doc.title: Benny Golson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Parents' jobs, the divorce, and a 99 percent Black neighborhood
summary: His mother sewed, his father worked for Nabisco then the gas company; they divorced. He began piano at nine, and the neighborhood was almost entirely Black.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: What was your father’s occupation? Also, did your mother work?

My mother worked as a seamstress, off and on. My father worked for the National Biscuit Company – Nabisco. In the beginning he worked there. I remember, because he used to bring cookies and things home that were day old, or old. Then after that he went to work for the Philadelphia Gas Company. Much later, they divorced. So it was just me and my mother in those years when I was a budding musician. I didn’t start as a saxophone player, though. I started as a piano player. I fancied that I was going to be a concert pianist. I was about nine then. That got quite a few chuckles in the ghetto. A concert pianist. Everybody’s playing the blues.

Let’s go back. You gave two very important things: how you got started on the piano, and you referenced your neighborhood as the ghetto. Was it a predominantly black neighborhood? Was it exclusively a black neighborhood?
It was 99½% black, because I remember I had a white friend that lived down the other end of the block. He was the only one in the neighborhood.
